subtopic: Class A, B, and C Shares
source_evidence: Class A shares might have a front-end sales load paid as a percentage of the purchase price, which may be discounted if certain criteria are met (e.g., a minimum amount is invested). Class A shares also have a 12b-1 fee, although this fee would generally be lower than the 12b-1 fee for certain other load bearing classes. Class C shares might have a 12b-1 fee and a contingent deferred sales load (CDSL) (a percentage-based fee that investors pay only when they redeem fund shares) for some period of time (often a year). Class B shares with a CDSL and a higher 12b-1 fee, but no front-end sales load were once relatively common. However, Class B shares are no longer widely available.
answer: Class A, B, and C are share classes of mutual funds, and their fee structures can differ. Class A shares might charge a sales load when you buy, though discounts or load waivers may be available; their 12b-1 fee is generally lower than that of certain other load-bearing classes. Class C shares might charge a 12b-1 fee and a deferred sales load when you redeem, and their 12b-1 fee is generally higher than that of other load-bearing classes. Class B shares were once commonly described as having no front-end sales load but a deferred sales load and higher 12b-1 fee; they are no longer widely available. These are possible features, not guarantees for every fund. Compare each fund’s fees and expenses, including how they may add up over the time you expect to hold the shares.
